evidence.claim: The Trinity Scenic Byway follows Highway 299 west from Shasta, outside Redding, to Blue Lake near Arcata.
evidence.quote: Follows Highway 299 west between the small community of Shasta on the outskirts of Redding all the way to Blue Lake near Arcata on the coast.

evidence.claim: The drive passes Whiskeytown Lake and follows the Trinity River through mountain country.
evidence.quote: passing by the Whiskeytown-Shasta-Trinity National Recreation Area and through the towns of Tower House and Whiskeytown as well as Whiskeytown Lake.

evidence.claim: Designated in October 1991, the byway carries the Forest Service theme “From the Valley Oaks to the Redwood Coast,” chosen to highlight plants and animals across its climate zones.
evidence.quote: Highway 299 was designated the "Trinity Scenic Byway" in October, 1991. The Theme of the route, "From the Valley Oaks to the Redwood Coast" was chosen by the Forest Service to feature the wide variety of plant and animal life that exists in the various climates zones along the highway.

evidence.claim: Near Del Loma, the river passes steep terrain and dense forest. The National Forest Scenic Byway designation covers this western corridor, while SR 299 itself continues east across northern California to Nevada.
evidence.quote: Surrounded by steep terrain and dense forest, Del Loma sits along the Trinity River

evidence.claim: Near Del Loma, the river passes steep terrain and dense forest. The National Forest Scenic Byway designation covers this western corridor, while SR 299 itself continues east across northern California to Nevada.
evidence.quote: The segment of SR 299 between Arcata and Redding is the Trinity Scenic Byway, a National Forest Scenic Byway.

evidence.claim: Near Del Loma, the river passes steep terrain and dense forest. The National Forest Scenic Byway designation covers this western corridor, while SR 299 itself continues east across northern California to Nevada.
evidence.quote: Route 299's western terminus is at US 101 at the northern edge of Arcata, and its eastern terminus is at the Nevada state line at a point east of Cedarville.

evidence.claim: The highway has repeatedly changed course to ease mountain grades and curves and to make room for Whiskeytown Lake.
evidence.quote: The actual road has been realigned many times, mainly to make easier grades and curves through the mountains, but also to make room for the Whiskeytown Lake reservoir.

evidence.claim: The basin began filling in 1962; some Whiskeytown buildings moved uphill while others remained underwater.
evidence.quote: the basin began to fill with water in 1962. Some Whiskeytown buildings were moved to higher ground, but others remain underwater.

evidence.claim: Elsewhere, old roadbeds remain visible beside SR 299, along with bypassed bridges, including an arch bridge dating to 1923.
evidence.quote: In many places, especially in Trinity County, the old roadway can be seen beside the new road, and there are even several bridges visible from the current SR 299 that seemingly connect nothing to nothing nowadays, one of which is an arch bridge from 1923.

evidence.claim: The Arcata-to-Alturas highway carried the US 299 number from 1934 to 1964.
evidence.quote: SR 299, from the intersection with US 101 to US 395 in Alturas, was U.S. Route 299 from 1934 to 1964.

evidence.claim: From Shasta, head west past Whiskeytown Lake toward Douglas City and Weaverville.
evidence.quote: In Weaverville, SR 299 runs concurrently with SR 3 southbound to Douglas City, where there is a rest area. SR 299 continues east away from the Trinity River into Shasta County, passing by the Whiskeytown-Shasta-Trinity National Recreation Area and through the towns of Tower House and Whiskeytown as well as Whiskeytown Lake.

evidence.claim: Beyond Weaverville, the river corridor links Junction City, Helena and Big Bar, then Del Loma, Burnt Ranch and Salyer.
evidence.quote: Paralleling the Trinity River, SR 299 passes through Salyer (where there is a rest area), Hawkins Bar, Burnt Ranch, Del Loma, Big Bar, Helena, Junction City, and finally Weaverville.

evidence.claim: At Willow Creek, Highway 96 branches off; continue on 299 through Six Rivers National Forest toward Blue Lake.
evidence.quote: The freeway ends in the city of Blue Lake as SR 299 continues east past the truck scales. SR 299 enters Six Rivers National Forest and intersects SR 96 at Willow Creek.

evidence.claim: Whiskeytown was a Gold Rush mining settlement first called Whiskey Creek Diggings.
evidence.quote: Whiskeytown was one of Shasta County's first gold mining settlements during the California Gold Rush of 1849, though at the time it was called Whiskey Creek Diggings.

evidence.claim: The post office opened in 1856, but federal officials considered the town’s name inappropriate until agreeing to it in 1952.
evidence.quote: The post office was opened in 1856, but the federal government didn't allow the Whiskeytown name to be attached to it because it was considered inappropriate. Finally, in 1952, the federal government agreed to name the post office after the town.

evidence.claim: Ten years later, the basin began filling behind the new dam.
evidence.quote: Construction of the Whiskeytown Dam began in 1960, and the basin began to fill with water in 1962.

evidence.claim: Some buildings moved to higher ground; others remain underwater.
evidence.quote: Some Whiskeytown buildings were moved to higher ground, but others remain underwater.

evidence.claim: The relocated store, a few residences and old mines above the water level are what remains of the mining settlement.
evidence.quote: All that remains is the relocated store, a few residences (mostly occupied by National Recreation Area personnel), and old mines that are above the water level of the lake.

evidence.claim: The cemetery moved too: all graves were exhumed and transported uphill during dam construction. President John F. Kennedy dedicated the dam in 1963.
evidence.quote: Whiskeytown Cemetery was moved during the construction of the dam. All the graves were exhumed and transported to higher ground.

evidence.claim: The cemetery moved too: all graves were exhumed and transported uphill during dam construction. President John F. Kennedy dedicated the dam in 1963.
evidence.quote: The dam was dedicated by President John F. Kennedy in 1963.

evidence.claim: At Junction City, the Trinity River heads northwest.
evidence.quote: The Trinity River runs through the town and heads northwest from there.

evidence.claim: The settlement began with a few cabins at the mouth of Canyon Creek in the 1850s.
evidence.quote: Junction City was established when a few cabins were built in the 1850s at the mouth of Canyon Creek

evidence.claim: Its first name, Milltown, reflected the number of mills.
evidence.quote: it was originally called "Milltown" due to the number of mills

evidence.claim: Mining also reshaped the river: the Arkansas diversion dam upstream was removed in 1857 so miners could reach gold deposits beneath it.
evidence.quote: In 1857, Arkansas dam was removed by the miners so they could reach the gold deposits beneath the dam.

evidence.claim: In 1861 it became Junction City for the transportation routes meeting at Canyon Creek and the Trinity River.
evidence.quote: in 1861 it was officially named Junction City since it served as a junction for several transportation routes at Canyon Creek and Trinity River.

evidence.claim: SR 299 now runs through the middle of town.
evidence.quote: State route 299 runs through the middle of Junction City.

evidence.claim: A centennial marker beside the Junction City store commemorates the community.
evidence.quote: There is one historical marker in Junction City to commemorate its centennial. [3] It is located next to the Junction City store.

evidence.claim: The town was formerly China Flat, a name associated with Chinese laborers from mining and lumber camps who settled here.
evidence.quote: Willow Creek's first non-indigenous settlers were Chinese laborers from the mining and lumber camps, which earned the town the name China Flat.
